children: Dow Inc.
expects to release more than $500 million of net working capital during the second half of 2026, providing an important source of cash as the chemicals maker confronts weak demand and softer pricing.

The forecast was included in slides prepared for a presentation by Chief Financial Officer Jeff Tate at the Morgan Stanley Laguna Conference. The presentation is scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. Eastern Time on Wednesday.
Dow

also said it expects third-quarter operating earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $1.5 billion to $1.6 billion, modestly below its prior expectations. The company cited weaker polyethylene pricing in the Americas and continued softness in construction and automotive markets.
For investors, the planned working-capital release may help cushion the effects of lower earnings and support Dow’s

efforts to reduce debt. Unlike cost reductions, however, releasing working capital generally represents a conversion of inventory, receivables or other balance-sheet assets into cash rather than a recurring improvement in profitability.
Cash generation takes priority
Dow

said it is actively prioritizing deleveraging with excess cash and has repurchased about $300 million of debt so far this quarter. The company has no substantive debt maturities until 2029, giving management additional time to strengthen the balance sheet.
Cash flow also benefited from the receipt of the remaining approximately $300 million in compensation from litigation involving NOVA Chemicals.
Dow

completed planned maintenance at several major assets during the third quarter and expects spending on those activities to decline in the fourth quarter. Management anticipates year-over-year improvements in operating EBITDA, cash conversion, net debt and rating-agency-adjusted leverage.

The combination of the NOVA payment and the projected working-capital release could provide Dow with more than $800 million of incremental cash during the second half, although the timing, sustainability and ultimate use of those funds will be important considerations for investors.
Chemical markets remain difficult
Dow

said July polyethylene prices in the Americas settled 10 cents per pound lower before stabilizing in August. The company is monitoring the effect of inflation and interest rates on demand, while cautious consumer sentiment continues to weigh on construction and auto markets.

There are some positive signs on the supply side. Dow pointed to shipping constraints in the Middle East and low water levels on Europe’s Rhine River, which could restrict industry supply. The company also said its global manufacturing footprint remains advantaged by favorable oil-to-gas spreads.

Dow has announced September price increases for polyethylene and other products in several regions. Investors will be listening for Tate’s assessment of whether those increases are gaining traction or merely meeting resistance from cost-conscious customers.
Cost-cutting program advances
Dow
also raised the expected in-year contribution from its “Transform to Outperform” program, which is intended to generate about $2 billion of benefits by the end of 2027.

The company expects approximately $700 million of benefits in 2026, including about $500 million during the second half. Dow said roughly 70% of 4,500 planned job reductions have been implemented, with nearly all expected to be completed by year-end. Those organizational changes are projected to contribute more than $200 million during the second half.

Additional second-half benefits are expected to include about $50 million from operational improvements at large production sites, more than $70 million from strategic sourcing and over $30 million from logistics and network optimization.

Dow also expects roughly $20 million from customer acquisition and market-share gains. The company is adjusting its commercial model to pursue demand from data centers and expects to reduce customer sample-fulfillment times by more than half.

The central question for investors is whether Dow’s self-help measures and improved cash conversion can offset a difficult pricing environment until industrial demand recovers. The projected working-capital release strengthens the near-term liquidity picture, but lasting upside will depend on higher operating earnings, stronger product pricing and evidence that the company’s cost reductions are sustainable.
